title: COBOL
subtitle: The business language of 1959 that still settles payments, pays pensions and prices insurance, from a first program to the mainframe.
description: COBOL (COmmon Business-Oriented Language) was designed in 1959 by a committee of computer makers, users and the United States government, drawing heavily on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC. It was built for business data: records read from files, exact decimal arithmetic on money, and long, readable programs that people other than the author can maintain. More than sixty years later it still runs a large share of the world's core banking, card processing, insurance, tax and social-security systems, mostly on IBM mainframes, and it is still standardised (ISO/IEC 1989:2023) and still compiled by current, supported compilers.

This course is for anyone who already knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. No mainframe access is needed. It begins with the four divisions and a first program, works through data definitions and picture clauses, fixed-point decimal arithmetic, paragraphs and PERFORM, tables, strings, files and reports, and ends with subprograms, modern COBOL, how professionals work on mainframes with JCL, CICS and Db2, and a complete payroll report.

To run the code, install [GnuCOBOL](https://gnucobol.sourceforge.io/), the free compiler from the GNU project (Linux distributions package it as `gnucobol`; the site links builds for Windows and macOS). Save a program as `main.cob`, then compile and run it with `cobc -x -free main.cob -o main && ./main`. COBOL has no official online playground. Every complete program in these lessons was compiled and run with GnuCOBOL 3.2 in free format by Lumenary's test suite, and the output shown is the output it printed. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Divisions, pictures and decimal money
levels.summary: Where COBOL came from and why it still matters, the four divisions of a program, describing data with levels and picture clauses, and the exact decimal arithmetic that money needs.

levels.title: Procedures, tables, strings and files
levels.summary: Structure a program with paragraphs and PERFORM, decide with IF and EVALUATE, search tables, take text apart and put it together, and read and write files and formatted reports.

levels.title: Subprograms, mainframes and a complete program
levels.summary: Split a system into called programs and copybooks, meet modern COBOL and the mainframe world of JCL, CICS and Db2, and build a payroll report from a file of employees.
